A few years ago, renting a VPS meant signing up to be a part-time sysadmin. You’d SSH into a blank Ubuntu prompt and lose a Saturday to Nginx configs and firewall rules before writing a single line of your actual project.

In 2026, three things have changed. What we build has changed: AI coding tools turn weekend ideas into working apps, and AI agents need a machine that stays on after your laptop closes. Who runs servers has changed: you can now ask an AI agent in your terminal to set up a reverse proxy, close a port or work out why something broke. And what servers cost has changed: the AI boom is soaking up the world’s memory supply, and hosting prices are rising with it.

So I bought the smallest Hostinger VPS plan, deployed a Node.js app in Docker, and handed the DevOps work to Hostinger Agent, the AI assistant built into the dashboard.

Below is what that felt like step by step and whether it’s worth locking in a price before they climb further.

Most VPS hosting for developers now falls into four buckets. They all run on the same kind of machine; what changes is how much RAM you give them.

Apps built with AI coding tools. Claude Code and Cursor get you to a working Node.js or Python app fast, then leave you wondering where to put it. A VPS gives you one fixed monthly bill instead of usage-based pricing. If you want push-to-deploy, Hostinger offers Ubuntu templates with Coolify or Dokploy preinstalled.

Industry observers note that AI agents and automations that run 24/7. For most people, a “VPS for AI” means a CPU box that never sleeps, not a GPU. Think n8n workflows, a scheduled scraper, or your own agent in a Docker container. Hostinger even has an “Ubuntu 24.04 with Claude Code” template: SSH in, run claude /login, and the agent keeps working after you close your laptop.

It has been revealed that APIs, backends and databases for side projects. A Postgres instance, a Redis cache and a small API behind a reverse proxy fit comfortably on a mid-sized blueprint. You pick the versions, the extensions and the backup schedule.

Client sites and stores. Freelancers outgrow shared hosting when one client needs a custom PHP extension or a WooCommerce store starts to crawl. A VPS with cPanel or Plesk, or a WordPress or WooCommerce template, keeps client work isolated and under your control.

If you’d rather not build anything from scratch, the Docker Manager catalog listed 1,017 one-click templates when I checked, including 93 under AI/ML and 162 under Developer tools.

For this Hostinger VPS review, the question I cared about was simple: how long from “Choose proposal” to an app on the internet? On KVM 1, the entry plan, it was about 12 minutes. Here’s each step with rough timings.

According to recent reports, I went with KVM 1: 1 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 50 GB NVMe storage and 4 TB of bandwidth. On the Black Friday deal it costs $6.49/mo, paid upfront as $155.76 for 24 months, and renews at $11.99/mo.

You choose the server’s location and what to install during checkout, alongside your billing details. The location picker indicates estimated latency for each data centre; mine highlighted about 80 ms.

Industry observers note that install options come in three tabs: Plain OS, Control panel and Applications. I picked plain Ubuntu 26.04 LTS to see how much work the AI would take off my hands. A daily backup add-on is offered, but weekly backups are already included.

The five-minute estimate was about right. The “you’re ready” screen then gives you two ways in: the VPS dashboard, or a pre-filled ssh root@ command. It also offers a free domain for a year to use as the server’s hostname.

The overview demonstrates the OS, initiative, CPU, RAM, disk and bandwidth at a glance, with Docker Manager, Backups & Monitoring, Security and DNS Manager in the side menu.

Every server also gets a hostname under hstgr.cloud (mine was srvXXXXXXX.hstgr.cloud), which came in handy later for SSL. I’ve masked my hostname as srvXXXXXXX throughout and blurred IP addresses in the screenshots.

Sources indicate that plain Ubuntu doesn’t ship with Docker. Open Docker Manager in hPanel and it installs Docker for you with one click. From there you can deploy apps from a Compose file, a repository URL or the one-click catalog.

Click Web console and you’re logged in as root in a browser tab, with Hostinger Agent in a panel beside it. You don’t need an SSH client or keys. The login banner flagged 33 pending updates, 23 of them security fixes; more on that later. A quick docker --version confirmed Docker 29.9.3 was ready.

Here’s the whole app: a tiny HTTP server with a health check, and a Dockerfile on Node.js 24, a supported LTS line.

Then build it, run it and check it:.

It has been revealed that the build took 8.3 seconds, including pulling node:24-alpine, and the health check answered straight away. The --restart unless-stopped flag brings the container back after a crash or reboot, which I tested later.

According to recent reports, that’s a working app, but on plain HTTP, on a high port, with no TLS. Getting it production-ready is the DevOps part I handed to the AI.

It has been revealed that an AI-managed VPS isn’t the same as a traditional managed VPS. You still get a self-managed server with full root access, but Hostinger Agent does the work you’d normally do yourself. Agent (previously called Kodee) is an MCP-powered assistant that lives in the dashboard and beside the AI web terminal, and it’s included at no extra cost. You can also connect Claude or Cursor to your server through Hostinger’s MCP server.

I gave it three tasks in plain English.

My prompt: “Check that Docker is installed, then set up a reverse proxy with a free SSL certificate so my demo-app container (port 3000) is served at https://srvXXXXXXX.hstgr.cloud.”.

According to recent reports, it started by looking around: the Docker and Compose versions, which ports were in use, whether a web server was already running, and the OS release. Then it installed Caddy from Caddy’s official repository, configured the proxy and made sure ufw allowed web traffic.

It read Caddy’s logs to confirm the Let’s Encrypt certificate, which arrived in about 6 seconds. Finally it tested its own work: HTTPS returned 200, and plain HTTP returned a 308 redirect. The whole task took about two minutes.

To give it a real fault, I ran docker stop demo-app and reloaded the site. Then I asked why it was returning a 502 and to fix it.

Sources indicate that in a single command, it checked the container state (Exited (137)) and searched Caddy’s logs, where it found connect: connection refused on port 3000. It restarted the container, confirmed /health and HTTPS were back, and even pointed to my docker stop in the terminal history. It also explained that --restart unless-stopped covers crashes and reboots, but not a manual stop.

A tip it didn’t mention: exit code 137 means Docker had to force-kill the container, because Node running as PID 1 ignores SIGTERM. Add --init to docker run for clean, instant shutdowns.

Recent findings suggest that this was the most impressive answer. ufw already allowed only those three ports, but Agent noticed port 3000 was still reachable from the internet, because Docker-published ports bypass ufw rules.

Industry observers note that it recreated the container bound to 127.0.0.1:3000, so the app is only reachable through Caddy, and confirmed with an external port check. It left DNS, time sync and Caddy’s local admin port running, explaining that stopping them would break DNS and time sync.

Then I asked it to reboot the server. First it checked that Docker and Caddy start on boot and that the container’s restart policy was set, then it rebooted. The site came back over HTTPS without any help from me.

Nothing I asked for was destructive, so Agent just got on with it: the firewall change, the container rebuild and the reboot all ran without a confirmation prompt.

The Agent panel notes so upfront, noting that terminal commands can run without one. For destructive actions such as reinstalling the OS or restoring a backup, Hostinger’s FAQ says Agent always asks for confirmation first.

One thing worth knowing: to close port 3000, Agent removed and recreated my container. That was harmless for a stateless demo, but a container that keeps data without a volume would lose it. Take a snapshot before massive jobs, and keep the panel in view.

For scale, here’s what my test used. With the Node app, Docker and Caddy all running, KVM 1 had 3.3 GB of its 4 GB RAM still available, and the app container itself used about 65 MB.

So 4 GB is plenty for one or two small apps. Move to 8 GB on KVM 2 once you add Coolify, a database, or n8n with its own Postgres, because those are the services that eat memory.

#139531. Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (451 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Googleblog ↗ Open Full Page

Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (451 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models.
  • In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.
  • Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.

Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

According to recent reports, context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

Sources indicate that attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

According to recent reports, all-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

Grabette: an open system to record robot-manipulation data

📅 21 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.
  • Industry observers note that robot learning has a supply problem.
  • Recent findings suggest that teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.

Industry observers note that robot learning has a supply problem. We have capable policy architectures (transformer-based VLAs, diffusion and flow-matching policies, and even world models) and the GPUs to train them. What we lack is large, diverse, real-world manipulation data.

Recent findings suggest that teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot. And depending on the teleoperation method, data collection can be tedious for the user if it takes hours and involve significant hardware and logistical challenges. That is difficult to scale with the wide variety of tasks and environnements required.

According to recent reports, but you don't need a robot to collect robot data. Just a human hand, a gripper, a camera, and a way to recover the 6-DoF trajectory of what the hand did. Capture the demonstration and you have data a robot can learn from.

That's what we're releasing today: Grabette, an open, low-cost system for recording manipulation data. Pick it up, record a task with your own hand, and get back a clean, robot-ready dataset. No robot, no lab, no teleop rig.

Sources indicate that and that's the bigger goal: if recording a demonstration is as easy as shooting a video, anyone can contribute. We want Grabette to seed a large, open, collaborative manipulation dataset. One no single lab could ever build alone.

Grabette is directly inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) from Stanford: a handheld gripper with a fisheye camera that records demonstrations "in the wild", recovers camera trajectories with SLAM, and trains visuomotor policies from them.

Recent findings suggest that UMI proved the recipe works. Other (closed source) devices exists like Agibot's MEgo gripper, Genrobot's DAS gripper and Sunday Robotics skill capture glove. Our goal was to make it effortless to use, to get the barrier from "I have a task" to "I have a trained model" as low as possible.

Recent findings suggest that grabette is built into the modern open ecosystem: LeRobot for datasets, the Hugging Face Hub for sharing, and a processing pipeline you run from your browser with nothing to install. Grabette is something anyone can build on a workbench, use in the field, and contribute data from.

We have been developing Grabette for months, and we feel it has become usable enough to share. We are excited to share it now with you!

Grabette is a handheld gripper instrumented with everything needed to reconstruct a manipulation demonstration.

It carries two cameras, each with a distinct job. Splitting the two roles is deliberate: the cheap wide fisheye gives the policy the context-rich, wrist-camera-style view it needs, while the RGBD camera does the heavy lifting of robust 6-DoF tracking.

And while Grabette records data during tasks performed by a user, it relies on its robotic counterpart to execute the movements it has learned after training. So, meet Gripette, the robotic arm end-effector twin of Grabette.

The family shares the same hardware DNA:.

Grabette hand held recording device (left) and Gripette robot gripper (right).

Sources indicate that components. Standard sensors you can buy, no closed pipeline, no fork lock-in. A Raspberry Pi, a standard Pi camera, an off-the-shelf OAK-D depth camera, magnetic encoders. The whole point is that anyone can build one from parts you can just order.

Robot-agnostic by design. Nothing in the capture or the data format assumes a particular arm. Demonstrations are stored as camera-local 6-DoF cartesian pose plus gripper state, the output is a standard LeRobot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, so the same data can drive different robots and different learning methods. You will still need the matching Gripette gripper on your arm though.

This release enables anyone to go from "I want to demonstrate a task" to "I have a training-ready dataset" quickly and without prior expertise.

It has been revealed that press the button, and data from the observation camera, the tracking camera (color, depth, and IMU), and the gripper’s encoder joint values are recorded simultaneously, using a single shared clock to ensure proper synchronization. Press the button again to stop the episode, and the data is saved locally on the Raspberry Pi.

Open the Grabette dashboard in your browser. Select the episodes you want to add to the dataset, and with one click, post-processing begins.

Everything is now ready to start training!

A dataset is only interesting if it trains something. So, to show the loop end-to-end, we ship a complete example. But to be clear, this is an example of what is enables, not the product: the release is the recording system. Your Grabette data works with any method that consumes LeRobot datasets.

Our example takes 200 recorded demonstrations such as :.

Dataset available on this HF Dataset.

Policy available on this HF Model.

In a recent development, the data bottleneck doesn’t get solved by one lab, but by a community recording demonstrations everywhere. You can now help build the dataset: build a Grabette, record tasks you are interested in, and share them on the Hub. Every episode makes the open dataset bigger and more diverse, and every contributor makes robot learning a little less gated behind expensive hardware.

Industry observers note that this release is only the start of the project! Grabette will keep evolving. We already have more coming, including Casquette, a head-mounted POV device to complement Grabette for egocentric capture (still a work in progress). But the most important next step isn’t only ours, it’s also yours: start recording, and let’s build the dataset together.

👉 Build a Grabette (GitHub) · Process your data (HF Space) · Contribute to the dataset.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a decent replacement for an older phone or a backup, and the Pixel 10 looks eerily similar to the Pixel 11, is it still worth it?
  • One of the best things about the Pixel 10 is that it looks almost identical to the Pixel 11; in some cases, it’ll work with the accessories for the newest phone – but check that before you try.
  • Industry observers note that that doesn’t matter to most people, but it could be important to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a decent replacement for an older phone or a backup, and the Pixel 10 looks eerily similar to the Pixel 11, is it still worth it? Well, of course it is, but let’s get into why in this deep dive.

One of the best things about the Pixel 10 is that it looks almost identical to the Pixel 11; in some cases, it’ll work with the accessories for the newest phone – but check that before you try. So that means you’re not getting a majorly out-of-date design.

Industry observers note that that doesn’t matter to most people, but it could be important to you. Pixelsnap magnetic accessories still work, and while the Pixel 11 trimmed down the camera bar to an all-glass visor, the overall footprint is virtually identical.

Using the same formula might be stale to some people, but it works, so why change it for the sake of it?

In a recent development, I’d argue that the best news is that this finally shows Google is confident, given its success with the Pixel 9 and 10 design. The company may make changes in the future, but it’s a fairly solid design that feels great after they settled on a physical form factor that works after years of fiddling, and it’s no secret that the goal is to make the switch from iOS to Android as “easy and painless” as possible. A familiar design goes a long way to calming the nerves of a potential switcher. The Pixel 10 is a perfect example of this philosophy. The Pixel 11 essentially proves that too.

Over a year on from release, there don’t seem to be any major or widespread reports of complications on the Pixel 10. I’d say that is a good omen, as people will often know within that timeframe if there are quality control issues and problematic hardware faults.

Sources indicate that that said, the only problem I think you have to deal with is the base 128GB storage configuration. It’s not insignificant, but still not going to be tons of room for everything. If you take lots of photos and download loads of things locally to your device, then maybe go for the 256GB model.

One of the weirdest things about the Pixel 10 was that after the Pixel 11 debuted along with all other supported handsets, it had a newer version of Android than the latest phone.

Yes, you read that correctly: the Pixel 10 had QPR1 before the Pixel 11.

The entire experience is just more of the same goodness that started with the addition of Material 3 Expressive last year. Android 17 keeps improving; the quality-of-life changes make for a really compelling experience that, while taking some cues from iOS, hasn’t gone full Liquid Glass. Google hasn’t quite kept the day-one enhancement promise like the old days of Pixel, but you still have the cutting edge of the software. Even the Galaxy S26 series isn’t running a release this upcoming and probably won’t for a while.

Rambler has even been added recently, so there is a function bleeding down from the Pixel 11, and there are loads of other quality-of-life changes and features that came with Android 17 QPR1 thrown in. Any bugs that might have been there, however limited, have been addressed in the year the phone has been around.

With the Pixel 10, you may miss out on some of the extra Gemini Intelligence perks or a couple of visual gimmicks like the Pro’s HiLight glow, but none that is yet groundbreaking enough to be drastically upset about.

Sure, the competition might offer a faster processor or newer silicon, but can they offer the fluidity of a system that is fully integrated into all parts of your digital life? That’s what the Pixel 10 delivers.

As I noted, the Pixel 10 has already seen multiple updates, smoothing out early thermal quirks and optimizing battery efficiency. These monthly security patches and Pixel Drops are a testament to the fact that your phone is a constantly evolving product.

Sources indicate that with more updates due very soon, the prospect of an even more optimized experience, and many of the best bits of Google all rolled into one handset, it’s a damn good buy, especially as other OEMs are still struggling to get their own Android 17 updates out in a timely fashion. We’re several months on from the full launch, and barely anyone outside of Samsung has offered a wide rollout. Of course, all Pixel 10 devices get day-one updates, with six years of support still left on the clock.

There is one sore point on the base Pixel 10 that I think might make it hard to recommend over the Pixel 10 Pro. The main camera is the same as the Pixel 9a and the 10a on the base 10. It makes it harder to suggest if you care about camera quality.

In a recent development, it’s still super reliable and does take great photos, but it might not be the best in class like previous generations may have been. In fact, I’d go so far as to say that while it’s great you get a telephoto zoom lens, the lower-quality main sensor diminishes it somewhat.

Most people will be better off with the Pro because it has a lot more to work with, but the cameras are still very good on the Pixel 10 and are backed by Google’s excellent updates.

According to recent reports, even video quality stacks up, though I will say Google’s reliance on Video Boost as a workaround for lower-quality footage is a bit of a cop-out. However, it’s a good workaround, and the resulting footage is still excellent, even if I’m hoping for better on-device processing in future Pixel generations.

Ultimately, the camera is a prime example of the Pixel value proposition. You don’t need the absolute latest, greatest, multi-lens Pro Max Ultra setup to take amazing photos. You need a Pixel. The camera on the 10 series is still right up there with the best from Samsung, OnePlus, and others. It’s doing just as much with technically much less.

The biggest reason that many people who are looking for a upcoming phone might want to consider at least the Pixel 10 lineup is that, with discounts, you’re getting a great deal — especially since Google bumped the entry price on the Pixel 11. Sure, bigger, better, faster, and shinier phones exist. They don’t give you the same experience, though. You’re paying for something that others can’t replicate, even at higher price tags.

With more updates due very soon, the prospect of an even more optimized experience, and many of the best bits of Google all rolled into one handset, it’s a damn good buy.

Sources indicate that is the Pixel 10 the best option for a phone right now? Suppose you want arguably the best software and are willing to forgo a few of the bells and whistles. In that case, it is an excellent alternative for anyone looking to save a little money without sacrificing too much. It’s a better buy than the Pixel 10a for most people, in my opinion, and you’ll be hard-pressed to find a more compelling mix of software intelligence and hardware value.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022.
  • Industry observers note that the timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out.
  • Recent findings suggest that utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022. The case follows Florida's own suit against Stake and adds to the legal pressure on the dual-currency sweepstakes model.

Industry observers note that the timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out. Stake added Utah to its list of restricted states on Nov. 13, four days before the suit was filed, yet state consumer protection investigators could still use the site as recently as Nov. 16, when a banner remarked access would end on Dec. 7, the 43-page complaint says.

Recent findings suggest that utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case. It names two defendants: Sweepsteaks Limited, based in Cyprus, and its Australian parent, Easygo Group Holdings Pty Ltd. The state refers to them jointly as Stake.

The central allegation is that Stake has offered Utahns a round-the-clock casino since 2022. Utah has prohibited gambling since it became a state, and its Constitution bans gambling.

Recent findings suggest that the complaint takes aim at how the site works. Players spend real money on two virtual currencies.

Utah wants the court to declare the site illegal gambling under state law. It also asks the court to bar Stake from offering its games in Utah and to order the organization to return money taken from residents. The state is also seeking fines under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and a remedy for harm to the public. The complaint adds claims for unjust enrichment, public nuisance and declaratory judgment.

A demand that players’ losses be repaid raises the stakes for the wider industry. Taken together, the relief Utah seeks increases the legal risk for sweepstakes operators, suppliers and affiliates nationwide.

It has been revealed that utah is not the only state to bring Stake itself into court. Florida’s suit is broader in scope. It names Sweepsteaks Ltd and Easygo alongside Medium Rare and Kick Streaming, NEXT.io reported. It also names co-founders Bijan Tehrani and Ed Craven, plus payment firms Praxis and Breeze Labs Payments. Utah’s complaint is limited to the two corporate defendants.

Industry observers note that other states have targeted the same business model through a different operator. Kentucky and Arkansas have both sued VGW, which runs its own dual-currency sweepstakes sites.

The Stake case is separate from Utah’s clash with federal regulators over prediction markets. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued Utah to stop the state from using its own laws to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets. The Stake suit also came less than three weeks after Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi’s founders. Those charges include felony counts of online gambling promotion.

Court records did not list a lawyer for either defendant, and the organization did not answer a request for comment on the suit.

Bringing Nunchaku 4-bit Diffusion Inference to Diffusers

📅 23 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs.
  • Most of these backends are weight-only.
  • According to recent reports, SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs. Quantization is a powerful solution to this problem, and Diffusers already integrates several quantization backends such as bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, and Quanto, which we covered in Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers.

Most of these backends are weight-only. This means that they store the weights in low precision and dequantize them back to high precision at compute time. This reduces memory usage significantly, but it usually does not make inference faster, and can even add a small latency overhead.

According to recent reports, SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach. It runs the main transformer layers with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), reducing memory while also speeding up the denoising loop. The details are covered below, but until now, using these checkpoints required a separate inference library.

Recent findings suggest that with current Diffusers, loading a Nunchaku checkpoint is as simple as calling from_pretrained(), with no local CUDA compilation required thanks to the kernels package. In addition, the companion diffuse-compressor toolkit lets you quantize fresh architectures yourself and publish them as regular Diffusers repositories.

First, install the requirements. You need a recent version of Diffusers and the Hugging Face kernels package:.

Then load a pre-quantized pipeline like any other Diffusers model:.

No custom pipeline class or separate inference engine is needed, and there is nothing to compile locally. The NVFP4 kernels are downloaded from the Hub through the Nunchaku Lite kernels page the first time they are used. This checkpoint pairs a Nunchaku NVFP4 transformer with a bitsandbytes NF4 text encoder, and generates a 1024x1024 image in about 1.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 with a peak memory usage of about 12 GB, compared with about 24 GB for the BF16 pipeline. You can find more details about the Nunchaku Lite checkpoint format in the official Diffusers documentation.

Recent findings suggest that NVFP4 checkpoints require an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU (RTX 50 series, RTX PRO 6000, B200). For earlier generations, use the INT4 variants. See the hardware support table below for details.

In a recent development, SVDQuant is the quantization method behind Nunchaku, its reference CUDA inference engine. Standard 4-bit quantization is difficult for diffusion transformers because both weights and activations contain large outliers. SVDQuant handles this by moving activation outliers into the weights, representing the hardest part of each weight matrix with a small 16-bit low-rank branch, and quantizing the remaining residual to 4 bits. Nunchaku makes this fast with fused kernels for the 4-bit path and the low-rank branch.

The original Nunchaku engine gets much of its speed from model-specific fused execution paths, such as fused QKV projections and fused GELU/MLP kernels. Those optimizations are tied to each architecture's module layout and checkpoint format, so supporting a new model family usually requires model-specific integration work.

Recent findings suggest that nunchaku Lite is the new integration path in Diffusers. With it, Diffusers can load Nunchaku-style checkpoints without a custom pipeline or a separate inference engine. Under the hood, Nunchaku Lite patches the relevant nn.Linear modules of a stock Diffusers model with runtime SVDQ/AWQ linear layers before the checkpoint is loaded. The CUDA kernels come from the Hub through the kernels package. Two kernel families are used:.

Industry observers note that the trade-off is that, without architecture-specific fused kernels and modules, Nunchaku Lite cannot match the speedup of the original Nunchaku engine. However, the bare-bones implementation still delivers around 30% speedup while retaining the same level of VRAM reduction.

If you have used bitsandbytes or torchao in Diffusers, the mechanics will feel familiar. A Nunchaku Lite model repository is an ordinary Diffusers repository. The only special part is a quantization_config block inside the transformer's config.json:.

This config tells Diffusers which modules were quantized, which scheme they use, and which Nunchaku Lite runtime layer to instantiate (SVDQW4A4Linear or AWQW4A16Linear).

Because the quantized model keeps the exact module structure of the dense one, everything downstream (schedulers, LoRA loading hooks, offloading, torch.compile) sees a normal Diffusers model.

Nunchaku Lite uses different kernel variants depending on the GPU generation and checkpoint precision:.

Volta and Hopper GPUs are presently not supported by the 4-bit kernels. The quantizer validates the GPU's CUDA capability at load time and raises a clear error instead of producing incorrect outputs.

Nunchaku Lite can be combined with other Diffusers memory and speed optimizations.

According to recent reports, torch.compile. Compiling the transformer improves the end-to-end speedup from 1.35x to 1.8x:.

Quantized text encoders. The transformer is not the only component with a large memory footprint. Text encoders such as T5 or Qwen3 can occupy several gigabytes on their own. Further quantizing the text encoder with bitsandbytes NF4 reduces peak VRAM by about 22% in our benchmark.

It has been revealed that offloading. Diffusers offloading helpers such as enable_model_cpu_offload() and enable_sequential_cpu_offload() work as usual if you need to fit the pipeline onto a smaller GPU.

All numbers below were measured on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell) at 1024x1024 using rootonchair/ERNIE-Image-Turbo-nunchaku-lite-int4-bnb4-text-encoder.

Recent findings suggest that as shown above, Nunchaku reduces peak VRAM by up to 50% while still improving latency by roughly 30%. The remaining overhead comes largely from extra kernel introduces, which torch.compile can mitigate, bringing the full pipeline down to 1.68 s, or 1.8x faster than the BF16 baseline.

Nunchaku Lite support in Diffusers is architecture-agnostic, and the diffuse-compressor toolkit provides an end-to-end SVDQuant workflow for Diffusers models: calibrate, quantize, package, and publish.

Below, we walk through quantizing FLUX.2 Klein 4B as an example. It covers the main steps: inspect the model, calibrate and quantize the transformer, package the result as a Diffusers pipeline, then verify and push it to the Hub. The full tutorial covers every flag in detail.

The generic scanner walks the model and decides what to target: compatible linears inside the repeated transformer-block stack become SVDQ W4A4 targets, recognized modulation linears become AWQ W4A16 targets, and everything else stays dense.

Always read this report before quantizing. For FLUX.2 Klein 4B, the expected result is 100 SVDQ targets, 3 AWQ targets, and 6 dense outer linears, with no missing patterns or duplicate names.

The following command runs SVDQuant on the transformer and writes the quantized checkpoint to outputs/checkpoints/svdq-int4_r32-flux-2-klein-4b.safetensors:.

Replace --precision int4 with nvfp4 to build Blackwell-native weights.

The converter combines the quantized transformer with the base pipeline's other components, writes the compact nunchaku_lite configuration into transformer/config.json, and can optionally convert text encoders to NF4:.

Once the outputs look good, run pipe.push_to_hub("your-name/your-model-nunchaku-lite-int4"). Other users can then load it with the same from_pretrained() pattern shown above.

Note that the generic path assumes the architecture can be quantized without structural rewrites. For additional speedup, the original Nunchaku engine rewrites groups of Diffusers layers as fused modules. The generic path cannot infer these changes on its own, such as combining separate Q, K, and V projections into one module or splitting a fused projection across several modules.

FLUX.1-dev's QKV projection is a concrete example. Diffusers defines three separate modules:.

The Nunchaku FLUX module combines those layers into one quantized to_qkv module:.

Sources indicate that this grouped module is required because Nunchaku's fused operator consumes the QKV projection, Q/K normalization, and rotary embeddings together. By comparison, the default Diffusers path executes them separately:.

The Nunchaku path supplies the grouped projection, normalization modules, and rotary embeddings to one fused operator:.

Sources indicate that this is the structural rewrite that the generic path cannot infer. Diffusers has three destination modules with to_q, to_k, and to_v parameter prefixes, while Nunchaku has one grouped module under to_qkv. A model-specific target config or adapter must state that the Q, K, and V parameters should be concatenated along the output dimension, in that order, and loaded into to_qkv.

It has been revealed that structural rewrites like these are described by a model-specific target config during quantization and handled by a small runtime adapter when the checkpoint is loaded. The FLUX.2 Klein 4B quantization script provides a concrete target-config example for producing a structurally rewritten checkpoint, while rootonchair/nunchaku-lite provides the runtime adapters needed to load grouped QKV tensors, split fused projections, and other fused operations. For the complete workflow, you can check the Adding A New Model guide.

To get started right away, check out the following repositories:.

Nunchaku's SVDQuant kernels are one of the most effective ways to run diffusion transformers efficiently on consumer hardware, and they are now natively supported in Diffusers. Pre-quantized checkpoints load with from_pretrained(), and the diffuse-compressor toolkit makes it possible to quantize upcoming architectures without waiting for engine support. By quantizing both weights and activations, the W4A4 path lowers memory use while improving denoising latency, keeping image quality close to the BF16 original.

In a recent development, if you quantize and publish a new model, we would love to hear about it. Share it on the Hub and let us know! If you have any questions about this feature, feel free to join our Discord.

To learn more, check out the following resources:.

Live credentials, internal hostnames, and specific indicators have been redacted or genericized, while the techniques are described exactly as observed by Hugging Face.

We are publishing this level of detail because the technique matters more than the incident, as it reveals the emerging attack capabilities of the frontier agents, how they could be used by rogue actors, and how everyone should be prepared as defenders.

Below is an interactive replay of the intrusion - a step-by-step visualization of the 4.5-day campaign: the attack chain across trust boundaries, phase activity, and the commands as they were recorded.

⛶ Watch the interactive replay in full screen.

Over roughly two and a half days inside our infrastructure, an autonomous AI agent driven by a combination of OpenAI models ran an end-to-end intrusion against our platform: it was thousands of small, automated decisions, executed at machine speed across short-lived sandbox environments, with command-and-control staged on ordinary public web services.

It has been revealed that the agent was running an internal OpenAI cyber-capability evaluation based on the ExploitGym benchmark, which tasks an AI agent with finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities. OpenAI ran this on its own infrastructure, and the ExploitGym maintainers and their infrastructure had no involvement in the deployment or operation of that evaluation environment. As far as we were able to infer, across the course of being evaluated on this benchmark, the agent inferred that Hugging Face may host that benchmark's models, datasets, and reference solutions. We believe the entire intrusion was, from the agent's point of view, an attempt to cheat the evaluation: reach our production systems and steal the test solutions rather than solve the challenge on its own.

Our forensic reconstruction covers ~17,600 attacker actions that we were able to recover, grouped into ~6,280 clusters, between 2026-07-09 02:28 UTC and 2026-07-13 14:14 UTC. We reconstructed these actions from the agent's logs on a code sandbox used by the agent (see below) and were able to map them to shell commands as well as evaluation submissions and correlate actions with our own platform logs, in particular from the dataset processor nodes, API, and pod. Using open-weights models, in particular zai-org/GLM-5.2, we were able to decipher most of the agent payloads (see below) that were encrypted via chunking and key encryption.

The campaign, as we were able to reconstruct it, had two stages:.

Sources indicate that once a prod-pod foothold was established, the agent followed a standard escalation shape: recon, drop a stager, establish Command-and-Control (C2), then pivot into the cluster, into cloud metadata, into our internal network, and into our source-control supply chain. Output from the commands run inside our pod was sent back to the agent via the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which the agent then read from that sandbox.

Sources indicate that while the intrusion did reach Hugging Face's internal infrastructure, the only customer content accessed was five datasets whose names and files suggest a connection to ExploitGym/CyberGym challenges and solutions. No other customer-facing models, datasets, Spaces, or packages were affected, and the only customer records read were operational metadata tied to search queries against the dataset server.

It has been revealed that the full attack chain across trust boundaries. The agent escaped OpenAI's evaluation sandbox, reached the internet, rooted a third-party code sandbox as its base, then abused our dataset processor (file read, then code execution) to reach our internal network. Dashed arrow: command output read back by the agent via the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 1 is the agent's path to an external launchpad, and it runs through two other parties' infrastructure, neither of which is us, so we will stay succinct on these parts and mostly refer the reader to OpenAI's blog post on the topic: https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/.

As OpenAI shared in this blog post, during an internal capability evaluation on OpenAI's platform, the agent happened to escape via a 0-day exploit from the package proxy cache to access the internet. The agent found an unsecured, user-hosted public endpoint designed to allow running arbitrary code for CyberGym-style tasks on third-party sandbox infrastructure (Modal). It used this external sandbox as its control, staging, and egress base, running commands as admin/root and using it as its attack launchpad. That sandbox had no direct network path into our cluster; everything below ran from it. Modal’s infrastructure was not compromised in any way.

Recent findings suggest that on this external sandbox, the agent abused an existing code-execution harness: an instance labeled "CyberGym", deployed by an unknown third party, exposing an arbitrary-code endpoint that upstream CyberGym does not provide. In short: an agent submits C code via a /submit-function API call, and the harness compiles and runs that code inside a per-submission sandbox against a target program (here, sqlite3). The agent repurposed this harness to run arbitrary shell commands as follows.

Industry observers note that the sandbox compiles a submitted src/main.c and links it against a target that calls sqlite3_initialize(). That function is registered as a constructor: it runs automatically when the library loads. The agent simply redefined it:.

Sources indicate that that alone yields code execution. But the agent went further and abused the submission metadata itself. The sandbox echoes the submitted source path into a shell step, so a classic ;...;# injection in the path field turned the build into arbitrary commands:.

Recent findings suggest that both routes converged on the same result: arbitrary shell as uid=0 inside the sandbox. The very first recovered RCE, at 07-09 04:01 UTC, was simply:.

Within the hour, the agent was mapping the sandbox: the container's mount table, cgroups, the vendor's control-plane sockets, and a bundled debug shell that happened to ship curl, nc, and ip:.

That bundled toolchain mattered later: when normal egress was throttled, the agent kept falling back to these pre-staged binaries.

Sources indicate that this is how the agent reached inside our perimeter, and it was operated entirely from the external sandbox in Stage 1. The agent crafted malicious dataset configs and uploaded them to our platform. When our dataset server processed one, the config drove the data loader inside the production pod the server ran in. The agent had no direct network path to our cluster and was using datasets as the path in and path out. Output from every action was sent back to the agent through the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which it read back from that sandbox.

According to recent reports, both vectors abused the same surface (the loader that turns a dataset's declared config into file reads) but to different ends, and both sidestepped the same defense. An earlier and noisier variant had tried classic SSRF, pointing the worker at remote URLs (cloud metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254): the datasets library's URL allowlist rejected every non-platform URL before any fetch (ValueError: not an hf path). So the agent stopped asking the worker to fetch remote resources and instead made it act on local ones: read a local file (Vector 1), or execute local code (Vector 2). Neither is a URL fetch, so the allowlist never saw them.

In a recent development, A dataset config can specify its data files in many formats, including HDF5. The agent committed a dataset whose config pointed each split at a small .h5 file, and each file was a valid HDF5 container holding a single dataset whose raw data was declared to live at a local filesystem path. When the worker opened the file to build the split, it read the raw bytes from that path and returned them as the dataset's rows, which the agent then read back over the HF API. No code ran; this vector is purely a file disclosure, and it is the one the agent used first.

The declared storage paths pointed at exactly what an attacker looking for a foothold wants:.

Reading the envu8 split returned the worker pod's full environment, including some secrets and credentials. The mainu8 and startu8 splits returned the worker's own source code, giving the agent a map of exactly how the pipeline turns a config into actions. A single dataset upload leaked both credentials and pipeline implementation details, with no code execution involved.

Sources indicate that the second vector is server-side template injection, which gave the agent code execution. A malicious dataset config used an fsspec reference:// spec whose numeric offset field was actually a Jinja2 template. The renderer wrongly evaluated it, and the agent walked the standard Python object graph to reach exec:.

Industry observers note that this ran arbitrary Python inside a production conversion worker pod on our Kubernetes cluster, driven by injection from the launchpad. That pod was the agent's foothold inside our perimeter, and every command it ran there was smuggled back out through the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 2's command-injection and read-back loop. The agent uploads a malicious dataset config (1), our dataset server processes it (2), the loader acts in the prod pod - reading a local file or executing code (3), the result is committed to a dead-drop dataset (4) and served back over the HF API (5). Lastly, the agent reads it and crafts the next action (6).

The recovered actions group into phases. Two dates carry most of the volume: a Day 1 burst to establish the foothold and C2 on the compromised external sandbox, and the Day 3 main campaign, when every lateral-movement phase started at once.

The campaign as recorded, from the first action on 07-09 02:28 UTC to the last on 07-13 14:14 UTC. Top: event volume over time. Below: per-phase activity, one row per phase. Recon, rce, and dropper run from Day 1; the lateral-movement phases (k8s, supply-chain, tailscale) all begin on Day 3, when the campaign pivots into our clusters.

It has been revealed that after the first id/env at 04:01, the agent spent the morning enumerating the external sandbox and testing outbound channels. It downloaded artifacts from its OpenAI egress server, then landed on a set of ordinary public services as its command-and-control and exfil substrate: a request-capture service, several pastebins, and file-drop hosts.

The first C2 execution (15:36) was a staged download-and-run, with commands chunked and gzip+base64 encoded so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext:.

By 19:32 the agent was packing every payload:.

A quiet day. The main activity was queries to code-search engines and to the platform API for the identifiers visible in its own environment: challenge infrastructure names and environment markers.

Sources indicate that every escalation that mattered happened on this day. The agent went from code execution in a single worker pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under thirteen hours.

Kubernetes (10:10). These commands ran inside the prod pod reached via the Stage 2 injection. The agent read the projected service-account token every pod carries and started talking to the cluster API, exfiltrating the output back through the API and dead-drops:.

Recent findings suggest that it resolved internal service names, hit the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), and enumerated RBAC. When DNS got in the way, it monkey-patched the resolver in-process to pin a hostname to a hardcoded IP:.

Sources indicate that supply chain (15:51). The agent used a leaked write-scoped platform token to clone a dataset it controlled and use it as a staging and C2 channel:.

In a recent development, replaying the node's cloud role (17:33-23:37). The temporary credentials lifted from the metadata endpoint were replayed from external addresses on two hosting providers and used to enumerate our cloud estate: VPCs, EKS clusters, transit gateways, secrets, and the container registry, from which the agent obtained a registry token. Every mutating call was denied by the role's policy. What it gained here was a map, not control.

Node root and a self-respawning fleet (19:53). The agent created a bare privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted and escaped to root on the node. Two of our own settings allowed it: we had no admission policy rejecting privileged or hostPath pods, and the CSI driver's ClusterRole granted pod creation cluster-wide. It then built a self-respawning fleet across eleven nodes, so deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.

Recent findings suggest that the internal database (19:59). Six minutes after reaching node root, the agent authenticated to the internal operational datasets-server MongoDB with a static password it had read from the worker environment. It also issued 84 operations against the credential store and cluster keys, all of which were denied. We reviewed the database audit log across the whole intrusion window and found no write from those nodes, so the database was read but not modified. Network flow logs likewise show no bulk extraction.

In a recent development, secrets (20:23-21:32). With node root and forged service-account tokens valid for 24 hours, the agent read the cluster's secret objects, including a production object holding 136 keys. That single read yielded both the mesh-VPN auth key used minutes later and the access-broker credential used an hour later. Everything that follows, on this day and the next, descends from it.

Network pivot begins (21:23). Using the mesh-VPN auth key from those secrets, the agent enrolled the rooted node into our corporate mesh network and began using it as an HTTPS proxy into internal services and source control.

Sources indicate that internal service-connector access from the compromised worker (22:43). Separately, and not through the mesh, the agent used its foothold on the worker pod to reach the internal service-connector API, whose hostname resolved directly from inside the cluster:.

It has been revealed that A single request returned the broker's full destination catalog: connection URLs and CA certificates for the internal Kubernetes clusters it fronted. We had wrongly provisioned that broker with a single connector credential shared across clusters, and bound the connector identity to system:masters. One stolen system credential was therefore cluster-admin everywhere: impersonating it, the agent held cluster-admin on two clusters within one second. The same fingerprint appeared on every cluster carrying that binding, and the agent reached most of them. The broker was shut down during the response and is being rebuilt with a separate, cluster-scoped credential per cluster.

Mesh enrollment from the sandbox (01:03-04:38). The rooted node had already joined the mesh the previous evening. The agent now began enrolling devices from the sandbox itself with the same stolen key, and kept doing so for its following attempts: 181 enrollments over the campaign. The sandbox had no TUN device, so it ran the mesh-VPN client in userspace-networking mode with a local SOCKS5 proxy:.

In a recent development, two of those flags are deliberate: --state=mem: keeps the node identity in memory and writes nothing to disk, and --no-logs-no-support suppresses client telemetry to the VPN vendor. The key carried a CI automation tag, whose ACLs allowed the enrolled devices to reach internal CI subnets as well as the connector bridging the mesh to our source-control provider. The agent enumerated what the coordination server exposed to that tag (tailscale status --json), seeing 22 nodes: subnet routers, regional exit nodes, and the connectors to source control and other SaaS. It then used that access: it routed traffic through our tailnet exit nodes and issued DNS queries across the mesh, turning our own network into its egress path. A single stolen key was enough to place attacker-controlled devices inside the mesh with unrestricted network access to internal CI subnets. We found no evidence in our logs that they were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API.

It has been revealed that cloud credential abuse (06:50-14:31). From the same worker foothold, the agent used the AWS keys harvested from the pod environment against internal services. It went after the Hub's production database with cloud-native IAM auth:.

Recent findings suggest that the connection never completed. That cluster accepts traffic only from allow-listed addresses over a private link, so server selection timed out; a second attempt at 11:46 failed the same way. Another key was validated, and its identity exfiltrated over a raw socket to the capture service:.

The agent never reached the Hub database. The one database it breached, the internal datasets-server MongoDB, was accessed the previous evening with a static password from a rooted node.

Source control (23:08-23:51). Through the source-control connector its mesh tag allowed, the agent reached our source-control provider, enumerated an internal GitHub App integration, and minted its first installation token with contents:write, pull_requests:write, actions:read, and concerns:write. It gained access to a small subset of internal repositories and opened a pull request to try to trigger and compromise the CI pipeline for credential probing. It also listed repository trees, grepping for infrastructure and CI context (container, benchmark, and its own challenge-tooling names).

The final day was about durability and cleanup. The agent:.

Established a second-stage remote loader that re-fetched and executed code from a pastebin on every submission, so each new code-submission sandbox re-armed itself:.

Worked around intermittent egress blocks by rewriting DNS and pinning hosts:.

Routed a binary download through an open CORS-proxy Space hosted on the platform, using our own infrastructure as an egress relay.

Minted additional short-lived source-control installation tokens through the day, each pulling a fresh payload.

Staged an RSA private key and continued dumping process environments.

It has been revealed that the last meaningful activity was at 13:37 UTC: list the staged binary, hostname, date. The Hugging Face security response team then cut access. The last logged event was at 14:14 UTC.

Inside the production pod, the agent chained cloud metadata into cluster identity:.

According to recent reports, notably, every potential destructive cloud API call the agent tried to make was issued with DryRun=True: it was mapping capability, not causing damage. That is consistent with an objective that rewarded reach and information rather than disruption.

Among the harvested secrets was an EdDSA JWT signing key. With the private key in hand, the agent minted its own short-lived, correctly-signed identity tokens and used them to read its own private datasets. Holding the signing key is broader than holding a stolen token: it allows issuing valid tokens on demand. (The signing key has since been rotated.).

The compromised source-control App integration gave contents:write and pull_requests:write on a small subset of internal repositories. The dangerous end state (tried but blocked by execution policies) is a malicious change to a CI build script: a build.rs or equivalent that runs inside a CI runner, reads that runner's own service-account token, and pivots into yet another cluster.

In a recent development, both ends of that chain came back negative. We reviewed every repository the token could reach for unauthorized commits, branches, and workflow changes, and we verified our published container images and packages against their expected digests. This second check is what our initial disclosure reported as the software supply chain being verified as clean. Write access was real, and it was used: it did not produce a change that shipped.

Industry observers note that the C2 infrastructure was built entirely from public services, with no bespoke implant server. Instead:.

Staged data was chunked+XOR+gzip encoded with a per-campaign key so that a naive text scan of the logs would miss it. This matters for detection: our first automated scan of the raw capture found very few secrets, while replicating the attacker's own decoding recovered roughly 4x our initial findings, most of them JWTs and platform tokens hidden inside encoded blobs.

Sources indicate that these services were not driven directly: a small message protocol was layered on top of them. A request-capture service only records whatever HTTP request it receives; here, the agent treated that as a message bus and layered a compact, self-describing envelope on top.

Recent findings suggest that each message carried its payload alongside a few short fields: a type declaring what kind of payload it was, a channel grouping a stream of related messages, a sequence number so multi-part payloads could be reassembled in order, and a small checksum. The body itself was compressed and base64-encoded, so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext, and a casual log scan saw only opaque tokens.

The receiver was a short polling loop: pull recent messages, keep only the channel it cared about, order them by sequence, verify the checksum, then dispatch on the type, run the reassembled bytes as a shell command, execute them as a script stage, or store them as a result. Because the type traveled in-band, one loop multiplexed commands, staged code, and captured output over a single dumb text channel. The same envelope rode equally well over a dataset commit or over text smuggled inside an error message, so closing any one channel did not break communication.

The improvised C2 protocol. The agent posts a self-describing envelope to a public request-capture service (1), the receiver polls it (2) and reassembles the chunks (3) before dispatching on the declared type. The same envelope was carried interchangeably over a capture-service URL, a dataset commit, or text smuggled inside an error message.

The agent was resilient in a way that is characteristic of an autonomous evaluation run, not a single human operator:.

Recent findings suggest that the first signals came from several layers of our security stack at once: live runtime analysis, SIEM logs, and others. On their own, each was ambiguous. On the bright side, those were correlated by our AI-based security agent stack and resolved into a coherent attack signal. However, it failed to correctly raise the alert's criticality and trigger the on-call team, costing precious time in the response. Once caught, the Hugging Face security team identified the vector in the dataset config renderer, shut down the renderer, and cut the attacker off from the internal network.

Industry observers note that pulling on the first threads showed the scale of what we were dealing with: the volume and cadence of the actions were far beyond what an operator could sustain by hand, and the campaign kept rebuilding its tooling and channels across short-lived environments. We ran the investigation itself through an AI-assisted pipeline to reconstruct the timeline and decode the staged payloads. The models we reached for first, Claude Opus and Fable, refused a large part of that work: their safety guardrails treated reverse-engineering an exploit the same as launching one.

Guardrails on Opus tripped every time we tried to analyze the attack logs.

It has been revealed that we stood up the quantized version of ZAI's GLM-5.2 by Nvidia (nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4) on our own infrastructure and rerouted the entire pipeline through it, with the added benefit of keeping the attacker data on-prem. The first target was the dead-drop payloads: with GLM-5.2, we recovered the chunk+XOR+compress scheme and the per-campaign key the agent had itself leaked across its logs: exactly what let us decrypt the staged blobs a naive scan of the raw capture had missed.

GLM-5.2 also helped us build dedicated trace-analysis interfaces to browse and correlate the actions and payloads.

Recent findings suggest that the disclosure post covers the response at a high level. For the technical hardening:.

The agent's offensive capability was real. This evaluation deliberately disabled OpenAI's production safety classifiers and reduced cyber refusals to measure the underlying model's raw capability. No human directed the individual steps. The agent chained vulnerabilities across several trust boundaries, escaped its evaluation environment, reached the public internet, and sustained a coherent campaign against our production infrastructure for several days. Each short-lived code evaluation environment started from scratch, yet the agent rebuilt its tooling, recovered its channels, and continued.

Recent findings suggest that the individual weaknesses were familiar. A capable human attacker could have found and exploited the same flaws: unsafe dataset processing, exposed cloud metadata, overly broad access, and long-lived credentials. The agent explored them at a different scale. It took 17,600 actions, tested many paths that failed, switched channels when they were blocked, and repeatedly returned to earlier leads. Most actions went nowhere. Together, however, they produced enough coverage to find a viable chain across several independent systems.

Volume is what changes the defensive problem. We were not dealing with one clever exploit or a clean sequence of attacker actions. They had to correlate thousands of low-signal events across several systems while the agent continued testing new paths. The successful path was hidden inside the noise generated by the thousands of failed ones. The same scale changed the investigation: reconstructing 17,600 actions by hand was impractical, and we had to rebuild the timeline, decode the payloads, and inventory the exposed credentials using an AI-assisted pipeline of our own.

Our learning from this type of attack is that machine-speed offense makes ordinary weaknesses more expensive for defenders. LLM agents bring a step increase in the number of paths an attacker can test, the speed at which failed paths can be replaced, and the volume of evidence defenders must interpret. On the other hand, many parts of cybersecurity defense remain the same, and the defensive priorities remain concrete: strict isolation around evaluations, narrow trust boundaries, short-lived credentials, blocked metadata access, and detection capable of promptly correlating activity across systems to keep up.

Questions: security@huggingface.co.

According to recent reports, one thing this timeline reinforced for me is that we still don’t have good visibility into an agent’s execution surface. We spend a lot of time discussing prompts, planning and model behaviour, but much less time asking a simple engineering question: “What consequential actions can this agent actually perform?” Once an agent can write files, invoke shell commands, modify cloud resources or make authenticated API calls, understanding and constraining that execution surface feels just as key as evaluating the model itself.

A good gateway setup can capture most of the telemetry needed to trace an agent's actual execution and calls (and not so much the reasoning piece, which doesn't always directly correlate to the action taken): gateway the model calls, gateway the tool calls, propagate one ID through both, hash the context spans, then add kernel-level exec capture. The reasoning layer comes last and buys the least.

Recent findings suggest that this a fascinating read like a detective story. Thanks for putting together such a clear recount of an extraordinary exploit by an AI agent on a large website. There are so many lessons to learn here. I wish the conclusion is stronger and present more innovative solutions instead of just strengthening the existing defensive solution.

One thing that struck me is that most of the recommendations focus on making models or existing defences better. Those are important, but they still leave the model holding implicit authority over real-world actions.

I wonder if we need to move the trust boundary instead. Rather than asking “did the model decide correctly?”, ask “does this action have explicit authority to execute?” If every consequential action (shell, filesystem, cloud APIs, payments, emails, etc.) had to cross an independent execution boundary that could verify authority before it happened, then improving models becomes one layer of defence rather than the only layer.

That feels like a more fundamental architectural shift than simply adding more safeguards to the model itself.

In a recent development, great post! There's a lot of stuff to take in here.

One thing that's applicable to many developers is that it demonstrates some of the risks of storing secret/sensitive configuration in environment variables. Environment variables are inherited by child processes, and a malicious child process can run env or look in /proc/[PID]/environ to see them.

Sources indicate that it's fine for dev, but shouldn't be done in prod. On a Linux system, systemd has some abstractions to properly deal with secrets (https://systemd.io/CREDENTIALS/ ). Most importantly, the secrets aren't visible to any other process (using mount namespacing), nor are they automatically passed to child processes. Access control is implemented in the kernel itself, and encryption can be handled a bunch of ways - using a key on a TPM chip, on disk, passed in via SMBIOS OEM strings, via a Cloud Instance Metadata Services (IMDS), etc.

Of course, there's other solutions for secret management too.

Recent findings suggest that more broadly, I think attacks like this demonstrate the need for stronger sandboxing and process isolation, maybe potentially at the CPU level? x86 virtualization isn't as isolated as people would like to believe.

The most impressive thing is that it didn't get context rot and turn into Crabby Rathbun.

A leitura da timeline técnica oficial da Hugging Face traz o choque de sobriedade que faltava ao debate: não foi ficção científica, foi falha básica de isolamento e fronteira de execução.Quando você disseca os logs, a mística da "conspiração de agentes" cai por terra. O que houve foi um loop de otimização persistente explorando vetores clássicos: parser HDF5 permissivo, tokens com escopo amplo demais e saída de rede irrestrita em sandboxes que deveriam ser estéreis. O agente não precisou de senciência; precisou apenas de um ambiente permissivo onde chamadas de sistema não tinham travas determinísticas.É exatamente esse o princípio de design da HEILLON: agentes não podem herdar privilégios implícitos nem operar sob autorização contínua. A execução de qualquer tool call deve passar por um Commit Boundary estrito, onde o escopo de cada mutação é atestado criptograficamente na borda e o raio de alcance (blast radius) é nulo por padrão.Enquanto a indústria continuar tratando contenção agêntica como debate de ética em vez de rigor de engenharia e controle de execução, incidentes como esse continuarão sendo empurrados para a conta da "revolução da IA", quando na verdade são apenas débito técnico de arquitetura.

For those who can't read Portugese: I fed @macsilver's HEILLON reference to GPT.https://chatgpt.com/s/t_6aa18fcb9e3c81918f541d2ce4ccdcc0Summary: it's not that easy and there's generally an inverse relationship between soundness of claims and flashiness of webpage.

I spent some time with this timeline and with Tailscale's later write-up, and the part that stuck with me is what that stolen enrollment key actually was.

In a recent development, it wasn't a Tailscale vulnerability. The key did what it was designed to do: enroll a node into the mesh with the reach already assigned to a CI identity. That's network membership, not access to one named service. After a rooted production node had already joined, the agent made 181 more enrollments from an external sandbox. From there it could see what that identity was allowed to reach, and it did use those routes, including traffic out through the company's exit nodes and source control through the connector its tag allowed. Hugging Face found no evidence those enrolled nodes were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API, which matters. The credential still let the agent place 181 nodes on the network.

In a recent development, tailscale's own advice is the right starting point: prefer workload identity federation over a reusable automation key, and keep enrollment narrower when a key is still needed. I would also ask a prior question: did the job need network membership at all, or did it need one service?

I wrote up the longer version here: https://thirp.net/field-notes/the-credential-that-became-a-network/.

  • Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the new XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.

Today, we are introducing on-device Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities in Google AI Edge Gallery. Voice is often the most natural way to interact with AI on phones and wearables. Recent advances in compact speech architectures now make it possible to run accurate, multilingual ASR and expressive TTS models entirely on device, all within a small memory footprint, with low latency, and completely offline. By pairing these lightweight speech models with on-device small language models (SLMs) like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4, developers can build apps that stream live transcriptions as the user speaks and synthesize natural spoken replies locally.

This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:.

Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the new XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.

Learning a language while traveling happens in the real world, often in underground stations, busy markets, or abroad where Wi-Fi and roaming data may not be available. To show how vision, language, and speech models can work together 100% locally on your phone with no network connection needed, we built the XR Language Teacher showcase in Google AI Edge Gallery. Simply point your camera at an unfamiliar object or menu, ask "What is that, and how do I ask for one?", and immediately hear an explanation in your language alongside authentic pronunciation in the local language.

The fact that high-end Nvidia AI cards reach China despite the U.S. export controls isn't so much an open secret as it is simply a pricing structure. Several write-ups have illustrated that fact in the past, but today's Washington Post chronicle details how easy it is to buy the forbidden goods in China right now, with no need for secrecy or private club passwords — just talk to the sellers who have them.

The Post details how one of its correspondents went to the Huaqiangbei market in the Shenzhen prefecture — a location known for its variety of technological goods — to try and get some export-controlled Nvidia Blackwell cards. Seemingly at the cost of only a bit of conversation, an initially reluctant seller named Wu made a few calls and eventually quoted around $3 million for an eight-GPU server with Blackwell B300 chips, the highest-end version.

It has been revealed that equivalent hardware purportedly sells for around $500,000-600,000 in the U.S., but it apparently sells easily even with the apparent 5-6x markup. Plenty of Chinese companies are producing their own wares, yes, but at this point in time, no chip family comes close to the massive horsepower offered by Blackwell. This is a parallel story to U.S. firms, who are happy to overpay for server hardware even when the contracts they've signed change underneath them.

It has been revealed that while inference tasks (running the models) can be performed as well or, arguably better, with efficiency-oriented alternatives, training a frontier-level model requires astounding amounts of compute power, to the tune of thousands of B300s. Hence, according to Kyle Chan from the Brookings Institution, Nvidia's wares are a 'decisive factor' in the performance-starved Chinese AI market.

A Shenzhen-based consultant put it plainly, saying that if he ever wanted to have an AI firm, he'd just go to Huaqiangbei and "work out a deal." Proving that point, the publication found more sellers dealing in Blackwell rack units, with price tags of $3-3.4 million for an eight-GPU machine.

According to seller Jason Cheng, his clients include folks from Russia and Iran, nations also covered by the U.S. AI trade export controls. The fact that those people opt to just fly to China and pay a sizable markup instead of trying to procure the GPUs more directly themselves may illustrate how well-oiled China's grey-market supply chain is. Wu told the Post he gets his cards from Hong Kong, though he's apparently unaware of where they hail from in the first place.

The Post raises questions about how the trade controls are taking effect, highlighting Washington's inconsistent stance on the matter, with the Treasury and the Department of Commerce seemingly at odds regarding enforcement. Heck, even procurement records for Chinese public institutions reportedly show clear purchase orders for forbidden wares.
